Quick technical answers to Alex’s questions (TL;DR first, details after):

TL;DR:
- Use the Chat API for multi-turn and richer structured output; Completions can still work for single-shot prompts but Chat is recommended.
- Redwood supports JSON schema hints & a structured output layer — we validate server-side and surface schema mismatches in the response metadata; we also provide client helpers for strict validation.
- Streaming is implemented as chunked SSE/HTTP where tokens arrive incrementally; we recommend sending a schema_id with the request so the client can reconcile partial output and show optimistic UI (we include token-level metadata and a final validity flag).
- Tokenization: chat messages include role/name metadata and are tokenized according to model tokenizer; max_tokens is enforced on the generation portion (same billing semantics), but prompt size (context tokens) differs between chat vs completions because of message framing.
- Embeddings/rerank: recommended pattern is to do vector similarity recall with embeddings and then run a cross-encoder reranker (via a small dedicated model) on top for precision.

Details:
1) Chat vs Completions
- Chat API expects a messages array [{role:"user", content:"..."}, ...] and is better for preserving system/user/assistant roles and multi-turn context. Structured output tools (JSON schema enforcement or tool-calling) integrate with Chat more naturally.
- Completions accept a prompt string; simpler, but you'd need to manage role framing and multi-turn concatenation yourself.

2) JSON schema & validation
- On the server we can check generated outputs against a provided schema and return: validity: true|false, errors: [..], and a canonicalized JSON field when valid.
- We recommend the client perform a final strict validation and fall back to an explicit parse or safe-mode renderer if invalid.

3) Streaming semantics
- Streaming uses incremental token frames. We include a metadata frame at the end with final_valid=true/false and any parse errors.
- For UI, our suggested pattern: render tokens as they arrive but keep them inside a JSON-aware buffer; only expose the parsed object once final_valid=true. You can show intermediate partial text for UX but avoid treating it as authoritative until final.

4) Tokenization / max_tokens / stop sequences
- max_tokens parameter limits the generated tokens. For Chat, the prompt token count includes all message framing tokens; plan for additional overhead.
- Stop sequences are honored in streaming (the generator stops emitting tokens) and we return a truncated final flag in metadata. Be careful with stops inside structured JSON strings — test with your schema.

5) Embeddings + rerank
- Run fast approximate nearest neighbor recall (embeddings) to surface N candidates, then run a cross-encoder reranker for final ordering. If latency budget is tight, consider a smaller reranker model.

If helpful I can draft example request/response payloads for the chat endpoint showing schema_id, streaming frames, and final validation metadata (I attached sample-payloads.json).
